description:
In 1927, Einstein spent a week trying to prove Niels Bohr wrong.

They were at the Solvay Conference in Brussels, in a room with Schrödinger, Heisenberg and 17 Nobel Prize winners.

The argument was over whether the universe was predictable.

Einstein believed that if you knew enough about a system, you should be able to know exactly what happened next. Bohr argued that at the atomic level, sometimes all you could know were the probabilities.

Einstein kept coming back with new thought experiments meant to prove him wrong.

Bohr kept finding answers.

That probabilistic view became central to quantum mechanics, which helped scientists understand the atom, build semiconductors and eventually create the hardware modern computing runs on.

And nearly a century later, probability sits at the heart of AI too.

When a language model writes a sentence, it works through possible next tokens and their probabilities, one after another.

Einstein famously said, “God does not play dice.”

A hundred years later, some of our most important machines do.

And Einstein wasn’t the only genius who bet against the idea that won.

We pulled together 13 stories of some of technology’s biggest companies and what they almost got wrong.
